lessons.title: How a council works: Nicaea to Vatican II as historical events, and where conciliar authority rests
lessons.explanation: Objective: be able to describe an ecumenical council as an event with a human history and as an act of the Church's teaching office, to distinguish the authority of a definition from the authority of other conciliar teaching, and to say what 'reception' does and does not do. Begin with the historical fact, which is less tidy than the theological claim. Nicaea met in 325, convoked by the emperor Constantine and attended by a few hundred bishops; its creed used a word not in the Bible - homoousios, 'of the same substance' - to exclude Arius, and its aftermath was not peace but fifty years of exile and intrigue, with Athanasius exiled five times. Ephesus in 431 condemned Nestorius and gave Mary the title Theotokos; the synod of Ephesus in 449, later nicknamed the 'robber council', reversed the verdict and was annulled by the council that followed. Chalcedon met in 451 under Emperor Marcian, with roughly five hundred bishops, and produced a definition that confesses Jesus Christ 'in two natures, unconfusedly, immutably, indivisibly, inseparably [united]' - language chosen to exclude two opposite errors, one of which dissolved the distinction of natures and the other the unity of the person. Trent met in three interrupted periods between 1545 and 1563, its sessions displaced by war and plague, and answered the Reformation with canons that end in anathema plus a body of reform decrees on bishops, seminaries and the liturgy. Vatican I met in 1869-1870, was cut short when the Italian state took Rome, and had already seen the minority bishops leave before the final vote on papal infallibility, a vote whose definition nonetheless states that such definitions 'are of themselves, and not by the consent of the church, irreformable' (Pastor Aeternus, chapter 4). Vatican II met in four sessions from 1962 to 1965 and defined no new dogma at all; it issued two dogmatic constitutions, two other constitutions, and a series of decrees and declarations, and its most discussed conciliar act of clarification was not a definition but an explanatory note - the Nota explicativa praevia appended to the official Latin text of Lumen Gentium at Paul VI's direction, which states that 'the doctrine set forth in Chapter III ought to be explained and understood in accordance with the meaning and intent of this explanatory note'. So a council is: a gathering of bishops in communion with the pope; an event shaped by politics, travel and accident; and an act which may, or may not, include definitions. Theologically, the authority of the acts rests on Christ's promise of the Spirit's guidance to the Church and on the bishops' teaching office exercised in union with Peter, not on the size of the assembly or the power of its convener - which is why reception of a council by the whole Church is the fruit of its validity, not the source of it. What a council's authority concretely obliges is stated in Lumen Gentium 25: definitions are to be accepted with the assent of faith as irreformable, while other teaching by pope or bishops requires 'that religious submission of mind and will' whose measure is set by the character of the document and the manner of its teaching. The Second Extraordinary Synod of 1985 added the rule that governs how the last council's documents are read: 'It is not licit to separate the pastoral character from the doctrinal vigor of the documents', and, of all the councils together, 'The Church is one and the same throughout all the councils.' Where Catholics argue, and they do argue, is over how much of Vatican II's teaching is definitive and how much is authoritative but reformable application; the level of a given text is a question theologians and canonists dispute, but the conclusion that the council may be ignored is not among the live options.
lessons.example: Work one council in detail, then use it to test a modern claim. The case is Chalcedon, 451. Step one, the event: the emperor convoked it to settle a dispute that had already produced two rival councils; the bishops had before them Leo of Rome's letter (the 'Tome') and the acts of the annulled synod of 449; attendance and pressure both mattered, and the definition was finally produced after the assembly had been deadlocked. Step two, the theological content: the definition affirms one and the same Christ, Son, Lord, only-begotten, 'in two natures' without confusion, change, division or separation, in one person and one hypostasis. Every adverb is doing work against a specific position: 'unconfusedly' and 'immutably' against the collapse into one mixed nature; 'indivisibly' and 'inseparably' against a division into two persons. Step three, the act's kind: it is a definition, accompanied by canonical and disciplinary measures, confirmed by the pope and accepted by the Church in the following decades, though not without resistance. Step four, the reception, which is where the case becomes instructive: the Coptic, Syriac, Armenian, Ethiopian and other Oriental Orthodox churches did not receive Chalcedon, and they remain in a state of imperfect communion with Rome to this day. Their objection was not that Christ is two persons - they anathematise Nestorius - but that the language of 'two natures' as they read it qualified the unity of the incarnate Word, and they insisted on the formula of Cyril of Alexandria, 'one incarnate nature of God the Word'. Step five, the modern judgement: ecumenical dialogue since the 1960s has concluded that much of the dispute rested on divergent terminologies and on mutual suspicion rather than on a substantive difference of faith, and Catholic and Oriental Orthodox theologians have jointly stated as much in agreed statements; the schism nevertheless remains, and both sides have resisted pretending it does not. Now apply the case to a modern claim. A Catholic traditionalist argues: 'Since Chalcedon's formula was not immediately received in Egypt and Syria, and since reception is what really matters, Vatican II's documents can be treated the same way - simply not received.' The argument fails twice. It fails factually, because Chalcedon's definition was confirmed by the apostolic see and accepted by the overwhelming majority of the Church, and because the dissent was about the meaning of a formula the Church had defined, not about whether the council had authority. And it fails theologically, because Vatican I's sentence - definitions are irreformable 'of themselves, and not by the consent of the church' - rules out the premise that reception confers authority. Reception is what happens when the Church recognises and lives out what was true from the moment it was defined; it is a sign, not a condition.
lessons.question: A parishioner announces: 'Vatican II was only a pastoral council - it defined no new dogmas, so nothing in it binds me, and I am free to reject what Dignitatis Humanae says about religious freedom.' Which correction is accurate?
lessons.answer: The conclusion is ruled out by the council's own teaching categories and by the 1985 synod's rule. Lumen Gentium 25 requires 'religious submission of mind and will' toward authentic teaching even when it is not a definition, and the 1985 Extraordinary Synod stated that 'it is not licit to separate the pastoral character from the doctrinal vigor of the documents' and that 'the Church is one and the same throughout all the councils'; Dignitatis Humanae 2 teaches as doctrine that the human person has a right to religious freedom.
lessons.distractor: The parishioner is right: because a pastoral council defines nothing, its documents are advisory, and a Catholic who disagrees may set them aside without any consequence for his standing in the Church.
lessons.correction: Two errors are stacked here. The first is equating 'not defined' with 'not binding'. Lumen Gentium 25 sets out the grades: definitions require the assent of faith, while other authentic teaching, whether of the pope or of the bishops, requires the religious submission of mind and will - and the degree of that submission is assessed from the character of the document, its formulation, and the authority with which it is delivered, which is precisely why the 1985 synod's rule forbids separating the pastoral character of the documents from their doctrinal weight. The second error is the specific claim about Dignitatis Humanae, which is a declaration of the council, not a discussion paper: 'This Vatican Council declares that the human person has a right to religious freedom' and grounds it 'in the very dignity of the human person as this dignity is known through the revealed word of God and by reason itself' (DH 2). What remains genuinely arguable is not whether the document binds but how its teaching should be classified - whether it is definitive, or authoritative but reformable in formulation - and Catholic theologians have argued exactly that question since 1965, especially in relation to nineteenth-century texts such as the Syllabus of Errors. That argument is a live one and is treated in lesson 63. What the parishioner cannot do is use the council's lack of new definitions as a licence to set the council aside, which is a claim the Church has rejected and which no council in history has ever supported.

depth.definitions: Ecumenical council: an assembly of the bishops of the Church, in communion with the Roman pontiff, whose teaching on faith and morals is received as the teaching of the whole Church. Dogmatic definition: an act by which the Church definitively proposes a doctrine of faith or morals; the response owed is the assent of faith, and the definition is irreformable (LG 25; Vatican I, Pastor Aeternus, chapter 4). Religious submission of mind and will (religiosum voluntatis et intellectus obsequium): the assent owed to authentic, non-definitive teaching, whose measure depends on the character of the document and the manner of teaching (LG 25). Anathema: the formula of exclusion attached to conciliar canons, meaning that the teaching is proposed with the alternative of exclusion from the communion of faith; it marks a definition rather than a comment. Reception: the process by which the Church recognises and lives out conciliar teaching - a sign and fruit of validity, not the source of it, since definitions are irreformable 'of themselves, and not by the consent of the church'. Nota praevia (Nota explicativa praevia): the explanatory note ordered by Paul VI and appended to the official Latin text of Lumen Gentium, which the council's own terms require readers to use in interpreting chapter III's teaching on the episcopal college. Grade of authority: the level at which a text teaches - definition, authoritative teaching, prudential application - which must be identified before a text can be obeyed, criticised or defended. Anti-conciliarism (the traditionalist position) and conciliar maximalism (treating every conciliar paragraph as a definition) are the two failed extremes; each fails because it collapses the grades established in LG 25.
depth.mechanism: How does a gathering of bishops in a palace or a basilica acquire the authority to bind the Church in faith? The mechanism has four moving parts, and seeing them explains both the strength and the fragility of conciliar acts. Part one is Christ's promise: the Church believes that the Spirit guides her into the truth, and that the gates of hell will not prevail, which is why she can hold that her teaching can be protected from error in particular acts rather than merely being generally reliable. Part two is the structure of the teaching office as the council itself describes it: the bishops teach with authority in communion with the bishop of Rome, and the unity of the college with its head is what makes an act of the whole Church possible (LG 22-25). Part three is the act itself: the distinction between a definition and other authentic teaching is the mechanism's most important valve, because it allows the Church to teach firmly without defining, and thus to leave room for development in formulation while still requiring assent. Part four is reception: how the Church tests, lives and finally assimilates what a council has said. Reception is not ratification - Vatican I's sentence about 'not by the consent of the church' forecloses that reading - but no historian can write the history of a council without it, because the texts that shaped the Church's life are the ones the Church received. Two consequences follow that learners find hard. First, an assembly's authority is not automatic: Ephesus 449 was a real gathering of bishops and its acts were annulled, which shows that the college's authority is exercised in a determinate way - in communion with the see of Peter - and that a synod can fail. Second, a council's authority is not proportionate to the novelty of its content. Vatican II defined nothing and yet its two dogmatic constitutions, on the Church and on revelation, restate and deepen the Church's self-understanding in ways that have reshaped canon law, liturgy and ecumenism; the absence of definitions does not mean the absence of doctrine, only the absence of a particular act. The limits of this mechanism are worth stating: it produces graded obligations rather than a single switch, so a learner's hardest task is always classification, and it depends on the Spirit's guidance rather than on the sociological authority of numbers, which is why the Church has never treated a large majority as itself the mark of truth.
depth.secondExample: Take a contrast case from the Middle Ages where the machinery of conciliar authority was contested in a different way: the council of Constance (1414-1418). It resolved the Western Schism by deposing claimants and electing Martin V, and it also issued the decree Sacrosancta, asserting that a general council holds its authority immediately from Christ and that everyone, including the pope, is bound to obey it in matters of faith and in reform. Read through the mechanism, this is a test of part two. If a council's authority derives from its communion with the pope as head, a decree that subordinates the pope to the council has no standing; if authority derives from the assembly's representation of the Church, the decree stands. The Church's later judgement was that the decree does not have conciliar authority in the sense claimed: the decree was issued in a disordered situation with rival claimants, it was never confirmed in that form, and it was subsequently interpreted in a way compatible with the primacy - which is why the ultramontane reading prevailed at Vatican I four centuries later precisely in the sentence about definitions not depending on the consent of the Church. The lesson from the pair Chalcedon and Constance is that the question 'is this act authoritative?' cannot be answered by looking at the fact of the meeting; it requires the catalogue of the act's kind, the authority of those who issued it, the pope's relation to it, and the Church's reception, in that order. It is also a check on the naive reading of history in which everything ancient is normative and everything recent is suspect, since Constance's reform work is honoured while its purported ecclesiology was set aside, and Vatican II's teaching is honoured even though it defined nothing. Classification, not antiquity, is the instrument.
depth.mistake: The most common mistake is treating the two ends of the spectrum as the only options: either every conciliar sentence is a definition that must be believed with divine faith, or nothing outside a definition binds at all. Diagnose it by asking the learner to place three texts on a scale - Pastor Aeternus's definition of infallibility, Lumen Gentium's chapter on the episcopate, and Gaudium et Spes's paragraph on work and wages - and to say what response each is owed and why. A learner who puts all three in the same box has not yet used LG 25. The second mistake is confusing the authority of an act with its reception, either by imagining that a definition needs the Church's acceptance to be true (contradicted by 'of themselves, and not by the consent of the church') or by imagining that reception is automatic, which ignores the Oriental Orthodox churches and the long controversies over Chalcedon and over Constance. The third is the historical error of treating councils as if they happened by mail: ignoring the role of emperors, wars, travel, illness and the political order produces a docetic picture of the Church's life and then makes the actual messy events, such as Vatican I's interruption, look like evidence against the Church rather than the ordinary conditions in which she acts. A fourth, specific to this century, is quoting the Nota praevia as if it were a secret doctrine hidden from the faithful, when in fact it is printed with the constitution and its purpose is stated in its own first sentence: to be used for interpreting chapter III.
depth.application: Task, ninety minutes. Choose one ecumenical council from the list Nicaea, Ephesus, Chalcedon, Trent, Vatican I, Vatican II, and produce a one-page brief with five labelled sections. (1) The event: where and when it met, who convoked it, what interrupted or shaped it, and one human detail you can verify from a source. (2) The acts: list what it produced, distinguishing definitions from other teaching and from discipline. (3) Authority: quote one sentence of the act that shows what response it asks, or, if it issues no definition, state what LG 25 says is owed to teaching of that kind. (4) Reception: describe one difficulty in its reception and how the Church's later history handled it. (5) Application: state one sentence of the council's teaching that bears on a question you care about, and label its grade of authority in your own words. Model response and self-review rubric: a strong brief names the council's own terms rather than generalities; classifies each act and never labels a non-definition a definition; distinguishes reception from ratification; cites at least two documents by paragraph; and ends with a claim about the level of authority that the learner could defend against an objection. A weak brief lists dates from memory, treats all conciliar statements as equally binding or equally optional, or uses the phrase 'the Council Fathers said' without knowing which text it is quoting. As always, the assessment instruments in this course test retrieval and method, not mastery of church history, and this brief is practice in the level's central skill of classification.
depth.summary: Four claims to carry: a council is an event, shaped by emperors and wars and travel as much as by theology; a council is an act of teaching whose authority rests on the bishops' office in communion with the pope and on Christ's promise, not on numbers, politics or reception; the acts of a council come in grades, with definitions demanding the assent of faith and other authentic teaching demanding religious submission of mind and will, and no one may separate the pastoral from the doctrinal (LG 25; 1985 Synod); and reception is the Church's recognition of what was true from the beginning rather than the condition of its truth - while still being the historian's indispensable guide to which acts shaped the Church's life. With lesson 63's criteria for development and this lesson's grades of authority in hand, you can now do the level's work on documents. Lesson 65 applies it to the Church's teaching about other religions, where Nostra Aetate and Dominus Iesus must each be read at their own level and not flattened into one another, and lesson 70 will ask you to read one contested document in exactly this way and to state, sentence by sentence, what it does and does not require.

readings.title: The Definition of Faith of the Council of Chalcedon (451)
readings.note: Read the definition itself, near the middle of the page: 'This one and the same Jesus Christ, the only-begotten Son [of God] must be confessed to be in two natures, unconfusedly, immutably, indivisibly, inseparably [united]'. The surrounding acts show the event: the emperor's convocation, the rival council of 449, and the role of Leo's Tome. Translation: the Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers English text.

readings.title: Second Vatican Council, Lumen Gentium, 22-25, with the Nota explicativa praevia appended to the official Latin text
readings.note: Sections 22-25 are the constitution's own account of the episcopal college, the pope, and the grades of assent; the sentence about 'religious submission of mind and will' that the lesson quotes is in 25. The preliminary note of explanation appears as an appendix at the end of this page, introduced by the sentence that the doctrine of chapter III 'ought to be explained and understood in accordance with the meaning and intent of this explanatory note'. Reading it removes any excuse for treating the note as a concealed document.

readings.title: Decrees of the First Vatican Council (1868-1870): Dei Filius and Pastor Aeternus
readings.note: Read chapter 4 of Pastor Aeternus for the definition, including the clause that such definitions are irreformable 'of themselves, and not by the consent of the church', which the lesson uses against the idea that reception makes teaching true. The page's introduction also records the controversy that followed the definition and the withdrawal of some bishops. Caveat: this is a widely used English rendering; the Holy See serves Vatican I's constitutions in Latin and Italian at https://www.vatican.va/archive/hist_councils/i-vatican-council/index.htm.

readings.title: Second Extraordinary Synod of Bishops, Final Report (7 December 1985), sections 1-5
readings.note: The synod was called to celebrate, verify and promote Vatican II. Two sentences matter for this lesson: 'we also verify that the Council is a legitimate and valid expression and interpretation of the deposit of faith as it is found in Sacred Scripture and in the living tradition of the Church', and, on how to read the documents, 'It is not licit to separate the pastoral character from the doctrinal vigor of the documents', followed by 'The Church is one and the same throughout all the councils.' Caveat: the Holy See's synod archive does not serve this report in English, so this page is used for the English text; the report is also printed in the documentation of the 1985 assembly.

readings.title: Council of Trent, Session XXV (1563): decree on purgatory, on the invocation of saints, and on indulgences
readings.note: Read it as a specimen of conciliar form: a doctrinal decree stating what is to be held ('there is a Purgatory, and that the souls there detained are helped by the suffrages of the faithful'), an instruction that 'more difficult and subtle questions' be excluded from popular preaching, and separate decrees on invocation and on indulgences. visual.title: A council: event, act, authority, reception
visual.description: Four concentric rings around a single council, showing that the same meeting must be described historically and evaluated doctrinally, with the grades of authority drawn as separate doors on the act and reception drawn as an arrow that returns to the Church rather than back to the act.
steps: Outer ring, labelled EVENT: convoker, date, place, attendance, interruptions. Fill it with the two contrasting facts 'Nicaea 325, convoked by Constantine' and 'Vatican I, cut short when Rome was occupied in 1870'.

Second ring, labelled ACTS: a set of labelled boxes - 'definition' (Chalcedon's two natures; Vatican I on infallibility), 'other authentic teaching' (Lumen Gentium 22-25), 'discipline' (Trent's reform decrees), 'explanatory note' (the Nota praevia).

Third ring, labelled AUTHORITY: two doors from Lumen Gentium 25 - 'assent of faith' for definitions, 'religious submission of mind and will' for other authentic teaching - with a third small door marked 'prudential application, argue freely'.

An arrow from the Authority ring to a box labelled RECEPTION, drawn as a wide curve that returns to the Church, annotated 'sign and fruit, not the source: definitions are irreformable of themselves, and not by the consent of the Church (Pastor Aeternus 4)'.

A broken line from the Reception box to a greyed box labelled THE ORIENTAL ORTHODOX CHURCHES AND CHALCEDON, annotated 'non-reception of a definition is a fact of history that dialogue has clarified but not erased'.
